# Acute tonsillitis and pharyngitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Infections of the pharynx and respiratory tract > Acute tonsillitis and pharyngitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/wj0hcT)

---

## Summary

<u>Acute tonsillitis</u> is an inflammation of the <u>tonsils</u> that frequently occurs in combination with an inflammation of the <u>pharynx</u> (tonsillopharyngitis). The terms <u>tonsillitis</u> and <u>pharyngitis</u> are often used interchangeably, but they refer to distinct sites of inflammation. <u>Acute tonsillitis</u> and <u>pharyngitis</u> are particularly common in children and young adults and are primarily caused by <u>viruses</u> or <u>group A streptococci</u> (<u>GAS</u>). They are characterized by the sudden onset of <u>fever</u>, <u>sore throat</u>, and painful <u>swallowing</u>. Patients may also have tender, swollen cervical <u>lymph nodes</u> and tonsillar <u>exudates</u>. The disease is normally <u>self-limited</u>. However, if <u>GAS infection</u> is confirmed via <u>rapid antigen detection test</u> and/or throat culture, treatment with <u>antibiotics</u> (most often <u>penicillin</u>) should be initiated to prevent <u>rheumatic fever</u>. <u>Tonsillectomy</u> is a treatment option for recurrent and chronic <u>tonsillitis</u>, especially in patients with tonsillar <u>hypertrophy</u> that causes <u>obstructive sleep-disordered breathing</u>. <u>Peritonsillar abscess</u> and <u>parapharyngeal abscess</u> are serious suppurative complications of <u>acute bacterial tonsillitis</u> and require immediate treatment.

---

## Epidemiology

* Peak <u>incidence</u> [[1]](/library/yMYdrp)

* <u>Acute viral tonsillopharyngitis</u>: children < 5 years and young adults

* <u>Acute GAS tonsillopharyngitis</u>: children aged 5–15 years; rare in children aged < 2 years

* Peak season: <u>Acute GAS tonsillopharyngitis</u> most commonly occurs in winter and spring. [[1]](/library/yMYdrp)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Acute tonsillopharyngitis

* Viral (50–80% of cases): <u>adenovirus</u>, <u>EBV</u>, <u>CMV</u>, <u>HSV</u>, <u>rhinovirus</u>, <u>coronavirus</u>, <u>influenza</u> and <u>parainfluenza viruses</u>, <u>HIV</u>  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[3]](/library/Xn097g)

* Bacterial (15–30% of cases)

* Most common: acute GAS tonsillopharyngitis caused by <u>Streptococcus pyogenes</u>, also known as <u>Group A Streptococcus</u> (<u>GAS</u>) [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)

* Others: <u>Neisseria gonorrhoeae</u>, <u>Corynebacterium diphtheriae</u>, <u>Mycoplasma pneumoniae</u>, <u>Fusobacterium necrophorum</u>, Group C and Group G <u>Streptococcus</u> [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[4]](/library/CwcqOe0)

* Necrotizing (or anaerobic) tonsillopharyngitis (sometimes referred to as <u>Vincent angina</u>): A rare anaerobic and/or mixed organism infection that may overlap with necrotizing <u>periodontal disease</u>.  [[5]](/library/35YSPp)[[6]](/library/19c2me0)[[7]](/library/W9cPme0)[[8]](/library/d9come0)

* Recurrent tonsillopharyngitis and chronic <u>tonsillitis</u>: polymicrobial infections with <u>aerobic bacteria</u> (typically <u>streptococci</u>, <u>staphylococci</u>, <u>Haemophilus influenzae</u>) and <u>anaerobic bacteria</u>

---

## Clinical features

### Acute bacterial tonsillopharyngitis [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)




* Sudden onset;  of symptoms: <u>fever</u>, <u>sore throat</u>, <u>dysphagia</u>

* Significantly inflamed <u>pharynx</u>

* Pharyngeal and/or tonsillar <u>erythema</u> and <u>edema</u>

* Pharyngeal and/or tonsillar <u>exudates</u> (rare in children < 3 years of age)

* Palatal <u>petechiae</u>

* <u>Cervical lymphadenitis</u>

* Absence of <u>cough</u>

* <u>Acute GAS tonsillopharyngitis</u> can also present as <u>scarlet fever</u> with:

* <u>Strawberry tongue</u>

* <u>Scarlatiniform rash</u>

* Rarely, features of necrotizing infection  and/or <u>dental disorders</u> and/or <u>periodontal disease</u>  may be present (see “<u>Vincent angina</u>”).  [[5]](/library/35YSPp)[[6]](/library/19c2me0)[[7]](/library/W9cPme0)[[8]](/library/d9come0)





> [!TIP]
> Children < 3 years of age rarely develop <u>GAS pharyngitis</u>; <u>GAS infection</u> in this age group more typically manifests with <u>fever</u>, <u>lymphadenopathy</u>, mucopurulent <u>rhinitis</u>, and excoriated <u>skin</u> around the nostrils. [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)




### Acute viral tonsillopharyngitis [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[3]](/library/Xn097g)




* <u>Cough</u>

* <u>Coryza</u>

* <u>Rhinorrhea</u>

* Oral <u>ulcers</u>, <u>anterior</u> <u>stomatitis</u>

* <u>Conjunctivitis</u>

* <u>Diarrhea</u>

* Absence of <u>fever</u>





### Red flags for complications of tonsillopharyngitis [[9]](/library/DHb1sE)




The presence of any of the <u>red flag features</u> listed below may indicate suppurative and/or invasive complications of <u>acute tonsillitis</u> and/or <u>pharyngitis</u>, such as <u>deep neck infections</u> (e.g., <u>peritonsillar abscess</u>, <u>retropharyngeal abscess</u>), <u>cervical lymphadenitis</u>, <u>mastoiditis</u>, and rarely, <u>sepsis</u>. [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)




* <u>Trismus</u>

* Drooling

* Asymmetric <u>tonsils</u>

* Displaced uvula

* Unilateral facial swelling

* Muffled or “hot potato” voice

* <u>Clinical features of sepsis</u>

* <u>Immunosuppression</u>





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Trismus</u> and change in voice quality indicate the formation of potentially life-threatening <u>peritonsillar abscess</u>!

## Diagnosis

Recommendations in this section are consistent with the 2012 Infectious Disease Society of America (<u>IDSA</u>) and the 2009 American <u>Heart</u> Association (<u>AHA</u>)/American Academy of <u>Pediatrics</u> (<u>AAP</u>) guidelines on <u>GAS pharyngitis</u>.  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[10]](/library/oaY0ln)[[11]](/library/kobmXu)[[12]](/library/xwcEOe0)




### Approach  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[13]](/library/ywcdle0)




The <u>diagnosis of acute tonsillitis</u> or <u>acute pharyngitis</u> is primarily clinical.




* Clinical evaluation

* Assess for clinical features of <u>acute bacterial tonsillopharyngitis</u>, <u>acute viral tonsillopharyngitis</u>, and <u>differential diagnoses of acute tonsillopharyngitis</u>.

* Proceed to immediate treatment if <u>red flags of tonsillopharyngitis</u> or <u>clinical features of airway compromise</u> are present.

* Suspected <u>acute bacterial tonsillopharyngitis</u>: Consider diagnostic testing to identify and treat <u>GAS infection</u> and minimize its transmission and complications (e.g., <u>acute rheumatic fever</u>).  [[4]](/library/CwcqOe0)[[12]](/library/xwcEOe0)

* Consider deferring diagnostic testing based on a clinical scoring system, e.g., no testing if <u>modified Centor score</u> ≤ 1.

* Obtain a <u>rapid strep test</u> if indicated, e.g., symptomatic patient ≥ 3 years old

* Positive <u>rapid strep test</u>: <u>GAS infection</u> likely; proceed to treatment.

* Negative <u>rapid strep test</u>: Obtain a throat culture in children ≥ 3 years old and consider obtaining in younger children (not routinely required in adults).  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[14]](/library/j6d_kI0)[[15]](/library/Bedza60)

* Suspected <u>acute viral tonsillopharyngitis</u>: Diagnostic testing is not routinely recommended.

* Suspected <u>infectious mononucleosis</u>: Obtain either <u>EBV serology</u> or a <u>heterophile antibody test</u>.  [[13]](/library/ywcdle0)

* Suspected <u>COVID-19</u>: See “<u>COVID-19 testing</u>” for details.





> [!TIP]
> Routine testing for <u>GAS</u> is not recommended for children < 3 years old, as their <u>prevalence</u> of <u>GAS pharyngitis</u> and risk of developing subsequent <u>acute rheumatic fever</u> are both low. Consider testing only if specific <u>risk factors</u> (e.g., close household contact) are present. [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[13]](/library/ywcdle0)




> [!TIP]
> Testing for <u>GAS infection</u> is not recommended in patients with clinical features that strongly suggest <u>acute viral tonsillopharyngitis</u>. [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)




![Diagnosis of tonsillopharyngitis](media/f76ohl38jg37or7u5vja5p3v.jpg)

Diagnosis of tonsillopharyngitis




### Rapid strep test [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)




* Modality: <u>rapid antigen detection test</u> (<u>RADT</u>) specific for <u>GAS</u> <u>antigens</u>.

* Indications: first-line test in suspected <u>acute bacterial tonsillopharyngitis</u>

* All symptomatic children ≥ 3 years of age and adults (unless symptoms are suggestive of <u>acute viral tonsillopharyngitis</u>)

* Consider in symptomatic children < 3 years of age if there is a household or other close contact (e.g., daycare) with proven <u>GAS infection</u>.

* <u>Modified Centor score</u> ≥ 2 (if scoring has been used)

* Procedure: Swab the patient's <u>tonsils</u> and the back of the throat.

* Findings   [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)

* Identifies the presence of <u>GAS</u> (positive <u>RADT</u>).  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[16]](/library/7jX4by)

* Time to result: 5–10 minutes





### Throat culture for GAS




* Indications 

* <u>Confirmatory test</u> to definitively rule out <u>GAS infection</u> in symptomatic children and <u>adolescents</u> with a negative <u>RADT</u>  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[14]](/library/j6d_kI0)[[15]](/library/Bedza60)

* Lack of clinical improvement after 3–4 days despite <u>antibiotic</u> treatment [[9]](/library/DHb1sE)

* Recurrent or chronic <u>tonsillitis</u>  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[17]](/library/yHbdGE)

* Consider in adults with <u>risk factors</u> for invasive <u>GAS infection</u>.  [[18]](/library/cybaVw)

* Findings   [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)

* Causative bacteria and their <u>antibiotic</u> susceptibility (see “Etiology” for details)

* Time to result: 24–48 hours





### Clinical scoring systems [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[16]](/library/7jX4by)




* Rationale: Estimate the likelihood of <u>acute bacterial pharyngitis</u> based on clinical features alone.

* Example: the <u>modified Centor score</u>

* Clinical applications

* Identifying patients with a low likelihood of <u>GAS infection</u>, thereby minimizing unnecessary diagnostic tests and <u>antibiotic therapy</u>.

* The use of scoring systems to identify patients with a high likelihood of <u>bacterial pharyngitis</u> in order to treat empirically without testing is controversial.  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[11]](/library/kobmXu)[[12]](/library/xwcEOe0)





| <br>Modified Centor score [[19]](/library/M7bMmE)[[20]](/library/L7bwmE)[[21]](/library/ioXJb_)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Criteria |  | Points |
| Age | 3–14 years | +1 |
| 15–44 years | 0 |  |
| > 44 years | -1 |  |
| <u>Exudate</u> or swelling on <u>tonsils</u> | Yes | +1 |
| No | 0 |  |
| Tender or swollen <u>anterior</u> cervical <u>lymph nodes</u> | Yes | +1 |
| No | 0 |  |
| Temperature > 100.4Â°F (> 38Â°C) | Yes | +1 |
| No | 0 |  |
| <u>Cough</u> | Absent | +1 |
| Present | 0 |  |
| <br>Interpretation <br><br>* Score ≤ 1: no further diagnostic testing needed<br><br>* Score ≥ 2: Consider <u>rapid strep test</u> and/or throat culture.<br><br>* Score ≥ 4: Consider <u>empiric antibiotic therapy</u> (controversial)  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[10]](/library/oaY0ln)<br><br><br><br> |  |  |





![Modified Centor score for group A streptococcal infection](media/way11hfmhhcs5a7hw7px8hag.jpg)

Modified Centor score for group A streptococcal infection




> [!NOTE]
> Think of M-CENTOR to remember the <u>Modified Centor score</u> criteria: M = Must be older than 3 years, C = <u>Cough</u> absent, E = <u>Exudate</u> on the <u>tonsils</u>, N = Node enlargement, T = Temperature elevation, OR = young OR old.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Empiric antibiotic therapy</u> for patients with a <u>modified Centor score</u> ≥ 4 is not routinely recommended. [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)




### Additional laboratory tests




Not routinely indicated; can be obtained as supportive diagnostic evidence




* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>Inflammatory markers</u>: <u>CRP</u>, <u>ESR</u>

* <u>Antistreptolysin O</u> (<u>ASO</u>) <u>titer</u>

* Elevated levels suggest a previous <u>GAS infection</u>; not helpful to diagnose <u>acute pharyngitis</u>

* Indicated in the workup of nonsuppurative complications of <u>GAS tonsillopharyngitis</u> (e.g., <u>acute rheumatic fever</u>, <u>PSGN</u>).   [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)





### Imaging [[9]](/library/DHb1sE)




* Not routinely indicated

* Consider CT of head and neck if there is clinical suspicion of suppurative complications

## Treatment

Recommendations in this section are consistent with the 2012 <u>IDSA</u> and the 2009 <u>AHA</u>/<u>AAP</u> guidelines on <u>GAS pharyngitis</u>.  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[10]](/library/oaY0ln)[[11]](/library/kobmXu)[[12]](/library/xwcEOe0)




### Approach  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[13]](/library/ywcdle0)




* All patients

* Provide <u>supportive care</u>: e.g., <u>analgesia</u>, <u>antipyretics</u>.

* If <u>red flags of tonsillopharyngitis</u> are present:

* Consult ENT urgently.

* Identify and treat <u>deep neck infections</u>.

* Consider empiric IV <u>antibiotics</u> and <u>steroids</u> for patients with <u>signs of airway compromise</u>, and prepare for <u>difficult airway management</u> as needed. [[13]](/library/ywcdle0)

* <u>GAS pharyngitis</u> and/or <u>tonsillitis</u>: typically <u>self-limited</u>; prescribe <u>antibiotics</u> to prevent complications (e.g., <u>peritonsillar abscess</u>, <u>rheumatic fever</u>) and decrease transmission  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[25]](/library/57bimE)

* Positive <u>rapid strep test</u> or throat culture: Initiate <u>antibiotic therapy for acute GAS pharyngitis</u>.

* Negative <u>rapid strep test</u>: Wait for throat culture results; treat if culture positive.  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[20]](/library/L7bwmE)

* Empiric treatment (e.g., for patients with <u>modified Centor score</u> ≥ 4) is controversial and not routinely recommended.  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[10]](/library/oaY0ln)[[11]](/library/kobmXu)[[12]](/library/xwcEOe0)

* Advise isolation and <u>droplet precautions</u> until patients are afebrile and have received ≥ 12 hours of <u>antibiotic therapy</u>. [[26]](/library/n7b7mE)

* <u>Acute viral tonsillopharyngitis</u>: <u>self-limited</u>; continue <u>supportive care</u> and provide patient education.

* Disposition: Outpatient treatment is possible for most patients.

* Improvement can be expected within 3–4 days. [[9]](/library/DHb1sE)

* Reasons to return to seek care: Persistent or worsening symptoms





![Diagnosis of tonsillopharyngitis](media/f76ohl38jg37or7u5vja5p3v.jpg)

Diagnosis of tonsillopharyngitis




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Amoxicillin</u> therapy in patients with <u>infectious mononucleosis</u> can trigger a <u>maculopapular</u> and/or <u>morbilliform</u> <u>rash</u>. Reserve <u>antibiotics</u> for patients with confirmed <u>bacterial tonsillopharyngitis</u> (e.g., positive <u>rapid strep test</u> or throat culture), whenever possible. [[27]](/library/IWaY5j)




### Supportive care for sore throats [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)




* Ensure adequate hydration.

* Consider household remedies such as salt-water gargles.

* Consider oral topical <u>local anesthetics</u>: e.g., <u>benzocaine</u> lozenges, <u>phenol</u> throat sprays, compounded mouthwash.  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[28]](/library/FEcgxV0)

* Consider single low-dose <u>corticosteroids</u> to reduce symptom duration in patients > 3 years old.  [[29]](/library/b9cHNe0)[[30]](/library/X9c9Ne0)[[31]](/library/c9came0)

* <u>Analgesics</u> and <u>antipyretics</u> [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)

* <u>Acetaminophen</u> DOSAGE

* NSAIDS: e.g., <u>ibuprofen</u> DOSAGE





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>aspirin</u> in children due to the risk of <u>Reye syndrome</u>.




### <u>Antibiotic therapy</u> [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)




* Indication: patients with laboratory confirmation of <u>GAS infection</u>  [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[10]](/library/oaY0ln)

* Suspected anaerobic or necrotizing infection (e.g., features of infection with <u>fusobacterium</u> or mixed organisms): Consult a specialist (e.g., ENT or infectious disease) for <u>targeted therapy</u>.  (see also “<u>Deep neck infections</u>”). [[5]](/library/35YSPp)





| <br>Recommended antibiotic regimens for acute GAS pharyngitis [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <br>Drug <br> | Duration |
| No <u>penicillin</u> <u>allergy</u> | <br><u>Penicillin V</u> DOSAGE: treatment of choice | 10 days |

> [!WARNING]
> Mistakenly treating an <u>EBV infection</u> (<u>infectious mononucleosis</u>) with <u>amoxicillin</u> can lead to a <u>maculopapular rash</u>.

## Tonsillectomy

### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* Ambulatory <u>tonsillectomy</u> is one of the most frequently performed procedures in children < 15 years of age.

* In 2010, there were almost 300,000 cases in the US. [[1]](/library/yMYdrp)[[2]](/library/BMYzIp)





### Indications   [[1]](/library/yMYdrp)[[2]](/library/BMYzIp)[[33]](/library/PPXWUy)




* Extreme <u>hypertrophy</u> of the <u>tonsils</u> (“kissing tonsils” ) causing <u>obstructive sleep-disordered breathing</u>.  [[34]](/library/fAbkQw)

* Documented recurrent throat infections   [[35]](/library/HsbKwE)

* Suspected tonsillar <u>neoplasm</u>

* Chronic <u>tonsillitis</u>

* Consider in patients with any of the following:

* History of <u>peritonsillar abscess</u>

* <u>Allergy</u> or intolerance to multiple <u>antibiotics</u>

* <u>PFAPA syndrome</u>





### Procedure   [[1]](/library/yMYdrp)[[36]](/library/2GbTAE)[[37]](/library/UGbbAE)




* Total tonsillectomy

* <u>Tonsils</u> are removed with their surrounding capsule.

* Dissection is <u>lateral</u> to the tonsil in the plane between the tonsillar capsule and <u>pharyngeal muscles</u>.

* Subtotal tonsillectomy

* Subtotal removal of tonsillar tissue, leaving a margin of tissue on the tonsillar capsule

* Dissection is from <u>medial</u> to <u>lateral</u> in a stepwise approach to preserve the capsule.





> [!TIP]
> Admit children < 3 years of age and those with severe <u>obstructive sleep apnea</u>, <u>obesity</u>, or complex medical histories (e.g., <u>Down syndrome</u>, <u>congenital heart disease</u>, neuromuscular disease) for overnight monitoring after <u>tonsillectomy</u>. [[1]](/library/yMYdrp)

### Complications [[1]](/library/yMYdrp)




* Intraoperative: injury to adjacent structures, e.g., the carotid <u>artery</u>

* Postoperative

* <u>Pain</u>, referred <u>otalgia</u>, <u>nasopharyngeal</u> stenosis

* <u>Dehydration</u> from decreased oral intake

* Respiratory compromise  [[38]](/library/8EcOxV0)

* Bleeding: See “<u>Posttonsillectomy hemorrhage</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> Do not use <u>acetylsalicylic acid</u> for postoperative <u>pain</u> relief after <u>tonsillectomy</u> because of the increased risk of bleeding. Recommended <u>analgesics</u> after <u>tonsillectomy</u> are <u>ibuprofen</u> and <u>acetaminophen</u>. [[1]](/library/yMYdrp)[[39]](/library/iAbJjw)




#### Posttonsillectomy hemorrhage [[40]](/library/qEcC9V0)[[41]](/library/IEcYCV0)




* Background: The risk of bleeding increases with age, reaching up to 20% in adults. [[42]](/library/DEc1BV0)[[43]](/library/wEchBV0)

* Primary bleeding: occurs ≤ 24 hours after <u>surgery</u>

* <u>Secondary bleeding</u>: occurs > 24 hours after <u>surgery</u>

* Clinical features

* Bleeding can range from clot formation and oozing to active profuse hemorrhage.

* <u>Clinical features of airway compromise</u> may be present.

* Initial management

* Move patients to a monitored setting with <u>airway</u> and resuscitation equipment available.

* Examine the <u>posterior</u> <u>pharynx</u> for signs of recent and/or active bleeding.

* If any bleeding is visible (e.g., clots, oozing, or active hemorrhage), establish large-bore <u>IV access</u> and obtain <u>CBC</u>, <u>coagulation panel</u>, and <u>type and screen</u>.

* Consult ENT <u>surgery</u> early.

* Establish <u>NPO</u> status (at least until evaluated by ENT <u>surgeon</u>).

* Minor bleeding

* Small bleed that has self-resolved: Consider observation under ENT for 12–24 hours.  [[40]](/library/qEcC9V0)

* History of recurrent bleeding or visualization of oozing or clot

* Keep for observation with frequent clinical reassessment.

* Definitive management as guided by ENT (e.g., cauterization at the bedside or in the operating room).

* Active hemorrhage or history of severe hemorrhage: Evaluate and manage patients simultaneously using the <u>ABCDE approach</u> while urgently contacting the operating room and ENT for high-priority surgical intervention.

* <u>Airway management</u>

* Have the patient lean forward to keep blood out of the <u>airway</u>.

* Use gentle suction to remove blood.

* Prepare for <u>intubation</u>; anticipate a <u>difficult airway</u>.  [[38]](/library/8EcOxV0)

* If <u>clinical features of shock</u> are present, initiate <u>immediate hemodynamic support</u> followed by <u>emergency blood transfusion</u>.

* <u>Hemostatic measures</u>

* Apply ice to the neck

* Consider intravenous <u>tranexamic acid</u> DOSAGE [[44]](/library/EEc8xV0)

* Consider <u>lateral</u> pressure to the affected tonsillar bed with gauze

* Once intubated, pack the tonsillar fossa.





> [!TIP]
> Secondary <u>posttonsillectomy hemorrhage</u> typically presents ∼ 1 week after <u>surgery</u>, around the time the <u>eschar</u> (<u>fibrin</u> clot) detaches. [[45]](/library/O8cI5V0)

## Complications

### Suppurative complications of acute tonsillopharyngitis [[15]](/library/Bedza60)




* <u>Deep neck infections</u>

* <u>Peritonsillar abscess</u>

* <u>Parapharyngeal abscess</u>

* <u>Retropharyngeal abscess</u>

* <u>Otitis media</u>

* <u>Sinusitis</u>

* <u>Cervical lymphadenitis</u>

* <u>Mastoiditis</u>

* Infectious thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein (<u>Lemierre syndrome</u>)

* Definition: a severe, potentially fatal condition usually resulting from oropharyngeal infections characterized by infection of the <u>carotid sheath</u> vessels and <u>bacteremia</u>

* Etiology: most commonly caused by oropharyngeal flora (e.g., <u>Fusobacterium necrophorum</u>)

* Clinical features: <u>fever</u>, <u>respiratory distress</u>, <u>neck pain</u>, throat <u>pain</u>





### Nonsuppurative complications of GAS infection




* <u>Acute rheumatic fever</u>

* <u>Scarlet fever</u>

* <u>Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis</u> (<u>PSGN</u>)

* Pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococcal infections (<u>PANDAS</u>) [[46]](/library/3VXS8C)

* Definition: a rare disorder that is characterized by sudden onset or exacerbation of <u>obsessive-compulsive disorder</u> (<u>OCD</u>) and/or a <u>tic disorder</u> following infection with <u>S. pyogenes</u>

* Pathophysiology

* Not fully understood

* Preceding <u>GAS infection</u> results in an abnormal <u>immune response</u> with development of cross-reactive, <u>anti-neuronal antibodies</u>  [[47]](/library/RVXl8C)

* Clinical features

* Abrupt onset or exacerbation of <u>symptoms of OCD</u> and/or a <u>tic disorder</u>

* Possible additional behavioral changes: <u>enuresis</u>, <u>separation anxiety disorder</u>, regression in <u>learning</u> and handwriting ability

* Diagnostic criteria [[48]](/library/QVXu8C)

* Presence of <u>OCD</u> and/or a <u>tic disorder</u>

* Onset during childhood

* Acute onset and episodic course

* Temporal association with <u>streptococcal</u> infection

* Neurological abnormalities during episodes (eg, motoric hyperactivity, <u>choreiform movements</u> of fingers/toes)

* Treatment

* <u>Antibiotic</u> eradication of <u>GAS</u>

* <u>Cognitive behavioral therapy</u> and pharmacological treatment for <u>OCD</u> and <u>tic disorder</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Antibiotic therapy for GAS pharyngitis</u> can decrease the risk of <u>rheumatic fever</u> but does not affect the risk of <u>PSGN</u>. [[2]](/library/BMYzIp)




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Streptococcus</u> "ph"yogenes is the most common cause of bacterial pharyngitis, which can result in rheumatic "phever" and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.




References: [[3]](/library/Xn097g)[[49]](/library/hS0cz2)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
